candidate_triples: To be young is all there is in the world. They talk so beautifully about work and having a family and a home (and I do, too, sometimes) --but it's all worry and head-aches and respectable poverty and forced gushing. Telling people how nice it is, when, in reality, you would give all of your last thirty years for one of your first thirty. Old people are tremendous frauds.
Have you heard that it was good to gain the day? I also say it is good to fall, battles are lost in the same spirit in which they are won.

It is only the novice in political economy who thinks it is the duty of government to make its citizens happy. Government has no such office. To protect the weak and the minority from the impositions of the strong and the majorityto prevent any one from positively working to render the people unhappy, to do the labor not of an officious inter-meddler in the affairs of men, but of a prudent watchman who prevents outragethese are rather the proper duties of a government. Under the specious pretext of effecting the happiness of the whole community, nearly all the wrongs and intrusions of government have been carried through. “The power of this poet-likely-to-become president first won the world’s attention at the Democratic Convention in 2004. Even that event could have been described as “improbable” but it stands now as a fact of recorded history. Between that history-making speech and Presidential Candidate Obama’s bestselling books, Dreams from My Father and The Audacity of Hope, two things become clear about the power of eloquence. It is not simply melodious syllables or beautiful fury disguised as poetic art. In the hands and heart of a sincere individual seeking to serve the common good, it can represent truth, vision, and clarity empowered by strength, destiny, and intelligence.” --from The Rise of the Poet Most Likely to Become President

Railway termini are our gates to the glorious and the unknown. Through them we pass out into adventure and sunshine, to them, alas! we return.

We who have lived before railways were made belong to another world. It was only yesterday, but what a gulf between now and then! Then was the old world. Stage-coaches, more or less swift, riding-horses, pack-horses, highwaymen, knights in armor, Norman invaders, Roman legions, Druids, Ancient Britons painted blue, and so forth -- all these belong to the old period. But your railroad starts the new era, and we of a certain age belong to the new time and the old one. We who lived before railways, and survive out of the ancient world, are like Father Noah and his family out of the Ark.

Also in 1903, Mann abandoned his naturalistic style, which he considered \"mechanical\" and published two  novellas, \"Tonio Kroger\" and Tristan\" in another style, which he considered \"musical\".  As a  consequence, he was now popular both with the public that liked \"Buddenbrooks\" and with the intellectuals who liked the novellas.  In 1905, Mann married a woman he had been pursuing for two years -- Katja, the daughter of Pringsheim,  Professor of Mathematics at Munich University. In 1911, after a holiday in Venice was cut short by a cholera outbreak, and during which he had been fascinated by a beautiful young Polish boy in his hotel, Mann wrote about this experience in a novel that gained great popularity, \"Death in Venice,\"  serialised in 1912, and appearing as a book in 1913. In 1914, Mann began writing \"The Magic Mountain\", not published until 1924. After the publication of \"The Magic Mountain\",  Mann wrote the novellas \"Early Sorrow\" and \"Mario and the Magician\".  As the  political situation darkened in Europe, Mann's essays stressed the importance of tolerance, warned that the humane impulse in man was in danger of being stripped away, and pointed up the need for reason to balance popular enthusiasm. In 1929, Mann was awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature. In 1930, Mann spoke out against Nazism, giving a  lecture in Berlin titled \"An Appeal to Reason\".  He called for the formation of a united front by the middle-class intelligentsia and the Socialist workers against what he labeled the inhuman intolerance and fanaticism of the Nazis. Mann continued to speak out courageously in his essays and on lecture tours in Germany and throughout Europe. In 1933, while Mann and his wife were in Switzerland, Adolf Hitler became Chancellor of Germany.  Mann was warned by his family not to return, and settled in Zurich, from where he travelled widely in Europe and the United States,  giving lectures. In 1936, Mann's German citizenship was revoked, and in the same year, the University of Bonn revoked his honorary doctorate.  In 1938, the Mann's went to the United States.  Mann first took a post at Princeton University, then moved to Southern California in 1941.  Two years earlier, he expressed his continued admiration of Goethe in \"Lotte in Weimar\" (\"The Beloved Returns\"), which told of a hypothetical meeting between an aged Goethe and a lost love from his youth. In 1943, Mann began his most political novel, \"Doctor Faustus\", an allegorical story of a composer and his music, depicting  Germany's tragic history in the 20th century.
